[1] [2] Under the Bhonsles from the mid-18th century, Nagpur expanded as a key Maratha power base in eastern India, controlling territories in present-day Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, and beyond, with the dynasty fostering agricultural development and military campaigns until the Third Anglo-Maratha War led to British paramountcy. [3] [4] The British period marked Nagpur's transformation into a colonial administrative hub, with infrastructure like railways and civil lines developed to support governance over the Central Provinces, while the city also became a site for early Indian National Congress sessions during the independence movement. [5] [6] Post-independence, Nagpur initially formed part of Madhya Pradesh until the 1956 States Reorganisation Act transferred its Vidarbha region to Bombay State , which became Maharashtra in 1960, positioning the city as a regional political and economic center known for hosting Dr. B.R. Ambedkar's mass conversion to Buddhism in 1956 at Deekshabhoomi . [5] [2] These shifts underscored Nagpur's enduring strategic importance at the geographic heart of India , marked by the Zero Mile Stone erected during British rule. [7] Ancient and Early Periods Prehistoric and Archaeological Evidence Archaeological surveys in the Nagpur region have uncovered Paleolithic artifacts, including Acheulian handaxes and cleavers, from deposits within Nagpur city itself, evidencing early hominid tool-making and resource exploitation potentially extending beyond 300,000 years ago. [8] These findings, recovered from depths up to 20 feet, suggest sporadic human presence in riverine and upland areas prior to more sustained settlements. The most substantial prehistoric evidence emerges from the Iron Age megalithic culture, dated approximately to 1000 BCE, characterized by extensive stone circle complexes such as those at Junapani, located about 10 kilometers northwest of Nagpur , featuring over 150 menhir arrangements enclosing burial pits. [9] These structures, part of a broader concentration of around 300 megalithic sites in the Nagpur vicinity, include cist graves, pit circles, and menhirs up to 2 meters tall, indicating communal funerary rituals and social hierarchies among early iron-using communities. [10] Associated artifacts comprise iron implements like arrowheads, sickles, axes, and nails, alongside copper objects and coarse red pottery , reflecting technological advancements in metallurgy and basic agriculture . [11] Excavations at habitational sites such as Khopadi along the Nag River bank reveal Early Iron Age layers with posthole structures, lime-surfaced floors, and evidence of rice cultivation, pointing to semi-permanent villages sustained by the region's fertile black cotton soil and proximity to water sources. [12] [13] Surface explorations in the Kolar Basin, Nagpur district , have further documented scatters of lithic tools and pottery fragments, suggesting a transitional continuum from Neolithic-like stone-tool phases to the Iron Age , with cultural influences from surrounding Deccan megalithic traditions. [14] Megalithic burials at locales like Kalambha exhibit capstone cists and orthostats, containing urns, beads, and faunal remains, which collectively demonstrate an agrarian economy reliant on crop domestication and pastoralism , rather than extensive long-distance trade , as evidenced by the paucity of exotic imports in these assemblages. [15] This material record establishes the Nagpur area's integration into the Deccan plateau's prehistoric networks, where iron tools likely enhanced land clearance and productivity on the basalt-derived soils, fostering population growth and settlement persistence. [11] Classical Era under Satavahanas and Vakatakas The Satavahana dynasty exerted control over the Vidarbha region, encompassing modern Nagpur, from approximately the 1st century BCE to the 2nd century CE, as evidenced by coin hoards discovered in areas like Brahmapuri tahsil in Nagpur district . These include lead and potin issues bearing legends such as "Sri Satakarni," indicating local minting and political assertion amid trade networks linking the Deccan interior to coastal ports. [16] Inscriptions and associated stupa remains, such as those at Pauni near Nagpur, further attest to administrative oversight and patronage of Buddhism , with artifacts suggesting Nagpur-area settlements functioned as inland hubs for agrarian surplus and commodity exchange. [17] Following the Satavahana fragmentation around the mid-2nd century CE, the Vakataka dynasty emerged in Vidarbha by the mid-3rd century CE, establishing its core territory around sites near Nagpur , including the fortified settlement at Mansar identified as the capital Pravarapura founded by Pravarasena II (c. 4th century CE). [18] Under rulers like Pravarasena I (c. 250â330 CE), who expanded the realm through conquests, the Vakatakas centralized administration via land grants and brick monumental architecture, as seen in the expansive structures at Mansar featuring apsidal halls and terracotta plaques depicting royal motifs. [19] This era marked a shift toward Brahmanical Hinduism , with Pravarasena I credited in inscriptions for performing Vedic sacrifices and endowing temples, fostering cultural integration across diverse local polities. [20] Patronage extended to religious architecture, exemplified by the Rudra Narasimha Temple at Ramtek , constructed between 400â425 CE during the reign of successors like Harishena, featuring early stone masonry and iconography blending Vaishnava and Shaiva elements. [21] Cave complexes at Ramtek , with reliefs and structural remnants, reflect Vakataka investment in sacred landscapes, supporting priestly networks and agrarian expansion through irrigated settlements in the Nagpur plains. [22] These developments underpinned economic stability via control of cotton and grain trade routes, though reliant on feudatory loyalty rather than direct taxation. [23] Vakataka dominance waned by the late 5th century CE due to internal successions fragmenting the dynasty into branches, compounded by feudal revolts and incursions from neighboring powers like the Asmaka chiefs and early Chalukyas. [24] Lacking robust military consolidation, the realm succumbed to these pressures without significant Gupta intervention in Vidarbha , leading to localized power vacuums by the early 6th century CE. [25] Medieval Period Regional Dynasties and Islamic Influences The Nagpur region, historically part of the visaya of Nagpura-Nandivardhana in Vidarbha , experienced Rashtrakuta governance by the mid-10th century, as documented in a copper-plate inscription from Deoli in nearby Wardha district . This record details a village grant issued under King Krishna III in Saka year 862 (940 CE), illustrating an administrative framework centered on agricultural land revenues that funded such endowments to sustain temple economies and local elites. [2] Subsequent Kalachuri rule from the Tripuri branch extended over portions of Vidarbha between the 10th and 12th centuries, with epigraphic evidence including inscriptions at sites like Bargaon preserved in Nagpur Museum collections. These artifacts, dated to the Chedi era, reference land grants and royal patronage of Shaivite temples, underscoring a taxation system predicated on crop yields and feudal obligations that supported religious infrastructure amid regional power consolidation. Yadava overlordship from Devagiri encompassed Vidarbha in the 12th and 13th centuries, marked by efforts to fortify strategic locales against mounting invasions from northern sultanates, though archaeological traces of such defenses in the immediate Nagpur area remain limited to scattered hill fortifications indicative of both adaptive resilience and exposure to raids. [2] The advent of Islamic rule disrupted these Hindu polities following Alauddin Khilji's 1296 CE campaign against the Yadavas, triggered by the sack of Deogiri and extending Delhi Sultanate suzerainty to peripheral zones like Vidarbha , where tribute extraction and occasional plundering prioritized fiscal gains over systematic religious persecution . [2] Tughlaq consolidation by 1317 CE imposed poll taxes such as jizya on non-Muslim subjects, per contemporary administrative records, fostering intermittent local resistance and economic strain without uniform conversions in agrarian backwaters. Bahmani Sultanate thrusts into Vidarbha during the 14th to 16th centuries, splintering from Delhi's orbit, involved probing raids for loot and control, evidenced by residual forts and coin hoards, compelling chieftains to bolster defenses while highlighting the era's causal drivers of predation amid dynastic fragmentation. [26] Transition to Gond Dominance The decline of regional dynasties and the ebbing Mughal influence in central India's forested plateaus during the late 16th and 17th centuries facilitated the ascent of Gond tribal groups to political prominence, particularly in the Vidarbha region encompassing Nagpur . The rugged terrain of hills and dense woodlands provided natural barriers against centralized imperial control, enabling Gonds to govern semi-autonomously through localized clan-based authority rather than expansive bureaucracies. This geographic advantage, combined with the Mughals' overextension following conquests like the 1564 subjugation of Garha-Mandla, allowed Gond chieftains to reclaim and consolidate territories previously under nominal suzerainty . [27] [28] In the Nagpur area, the Deogarh Gond kingdom emerged as a key power, established in the 15th century by Jatba and expanding to dominate the Nagpur plains by the 17th century through strategic alliances among tribal subgroups. Unlike the more expansive Garha-Mandla kingdom to the northâwhere Sangram Shah (r. c. 1480â1530) unified disparate principalities by capturing over 50 forts and integrating Hindu administrative elementsâthe Deogarh state focused on Vidarbha's core, relying on kinship ties to mobilize resources. Rulers like those succeeding Jatba forged pacts with neighboring Gonds and adopted titles echoing Hindu kingship, such as " Shah ," to legitimize rule while preserving tribal hierarchies that included servile labor akin to slavery in forest clearance and warfare. [27] [29] [30] Administratively, Gond dominance hinged on pragmatic adaptations: kingdoms were segmented into garhs (fort-based districts) overseen by clan heads, who levied tribal militias for defense rather than standing armies, drawing on forest yields like timber, mahua flowers, and tendu leaves for revenue alongside rudimentary agrarian taxes. This system blended indigenous customary lawsâemphasizing communal resource sharingâwith borrowed Hindu revenue practices, such as land grants to Brahmins for temples, fostering limited cultural synthesis without erasing Gond animism or clan autonomy. Evidence from contemporary accounts highlights how such structures sustained self-sufficiency amid Mughal tribute demands, though they proved vulnerable to internal feuds; clan rivalries often precipitated fragmentation, as seen in Deogarh's intermittent succession disputes, yet these polities endured by repelling raids from Afghans and later Marathas until the early 18th century . [31] [32] [30] While critics, including Mughal chroniclers, derided Gond rule for its decentralized "tribal" inefficiencies leading to chronic infighting, this overlooks achievements in regional equilibrium: Deogarh's governance preserved ecological balances through regulated forest use and deterred larger invasions via guerrilla tactics suited to the landscape, maintaining de facto independence longer than more rigid Hindu states in the Deccan. Such stability stemmed from causal alignments between terrain, tribal mobilization, and adaptive governance , rather than egalitarian ideals unsubstantiated by records of monarchical courts and bonded labor. [28] [27] Gond Kingdom Establishment and Key Gond Rulers The Gond rulers of Deogarh established control over the Nagpur region in the early 18th century , transforming it into a core territory of their kingdom through strategic consolidation and urban development. Bakht Buland Shah , who had initially served the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb and adopted Islam to secure support against rival claimants in Deogarh, founded the city of Nagpur circa 1702 by amalgamating twelve pre-existing villages, thereby creating a fortified administrative hub suited to the region's hilly terrain and riverine defenses. [33] [2] This act reflected pragmatic state-building, leveraging Nagpur 's central location in Vidarbha for tribute collection and military oversight, amid the weakening Mughal suzerainty that had nominally claimed the area since earlier submissions like the 1635 Deogarh capitulation. [30] Bakht Buland's successor, his son Chand Sultan (r. circa 1706â1739), formalized Nagpur as the kingdom's capital, shifting from Deogarh to capitalize on its defensible geography and agricultural potential, which supported a population sustained by cotton and millet cultivation. Under Chand Sultan, the kingdom prospered through expanded irrigation and trade routes, evading full Mughal integration despite nominal tribute obligationsâa pattern of de facto autonomy rooted in the Gonds' forested strongholds and guerrilla tactics honed against prior imperial incursions. [2] [27] Chand Sultan's death in 1739 triggered succession crises, with an illegitimate claimant, Wali Shah, briefly usurping the throne before rightful heirs, including Burhan Shah (r. circa 1740âc. 1796), were installed amid fraternal rivalries. Burhan Shah, a grandson of Bakht Buland, inherited a realm shaped by generations of selective Mughal resistance, where Gond rulers had intermittently withheld tribute post-Aurangzeb's campaigns, relying on terrain advantages like the Satpura hills for evasion rather than open confrontation. [2] [30] This era underscored the Gonds' absolutist governance, prioritizing dynastic continuity over broader alliances, though internal divisions exposed vulnerabilities to opportunistic external powers. [34] Administrative and Cultural Developments under Gonds The administrative framework of the Gond rulers in Nagpur , centered around the Deogarh branch, operated on a semi-feudal basis, with the sovereign granting jagirs (land assignments) to nobles, military leaders, and retainers in return for tribute and military service . [35] Revenue extraction relied heavily on agrarian tribute paid in kind , typically a share of crop yields from cultivators, supplemented by levies on trade and artisanal production; this system , while rudimentary, supported proto-urban nucleation around Nagpur by integrating local castes into revenue collection roles, though it imposed variable burdens on peasant households without standardized assessment until influences from neighboring Gond polities like Chanda introduced more defined apportionments. [36] [27] Culturally, Gond patronage extended to religious infrastructure, notably enhancing sites like the Ramtek temple complex, which served as a focal point for rituals blending indigenous animism with Hindu devotion, thereby sustaining festivals such as harvest gatherings involving communal feasts, animal sacrifices, and liquor consumption to invoke agricultural prosperity. [37] [38] Irrigation works, including tanks and channels, were constructed to bolster rice cultivation in the Nagpur plains, reflecting adaptive resource management but dependent on mobilized village labor that strained local economies during lean seasons. [27] This isolation in forested uplands preserved core Gond patrilineal sagas (clans) and exogamous practices, minimizing external disruptions to tribal hierarchies, yet it curtailed diffusion of metallurgical or firearm innovations from Mughal peripheries, rendering defenses reliant on hill forts vulnerable to organized incursions by the 18th century . [36] [35] Bhonsle Maratha Era Conquest by Raghoji Bhonsle I Raghoji Bhonsle I, a Maratha commander initially serving under Chhatrapati Shahu, exploited the internal dissensions plaguing the fragmented Gond kingdoms of Devagad, Gadha-Mandla, Chanda, and Chhattisgarh to launch targeted campaigns of subjugation beginning in the 1730s. [39] These kingdoms suffered from succession disputes and factional strife, such as the conflict between Wali Shah and Mir Bahadar in Devagad, where Rani Ratan Kuvar sought external aid against usurpation. [39] In 1737, Raghoji received a sanad from the rani granting him one-third of Devagad territories and an indemnity of 10 lakh rupees in exchange for military support, marking the initial foothold that enabled full control by 1748 through relocation of Gond rulers' heirs under his oversight. [39] The conquest of Nagpur proper accelerated after the 1739 death of Chand Sultan, ruler of the Devagad Gond kingdom, which triggered contending factions to invite Raghoji's intervention; he ousted and replaced the sultan's sons, Burhan Shah and Akbar Shah, establishing Maratha authority by 1743 amid the resulting power vacuum . [40] Military operations involved sieges, such as the 22-day blockade of Bhandara fort ended by treachery, and battles like the rout of Gond forces near Sonbardi-Mirnagar, where many drowned in the Wainganga River during retreat. [39] Further expansion targeted Deogarh and Chanda, with Pauni captured after direct combat against its thanedar, culminating in effective control over these districts by 1751 through a combination of force and sanads authorizing perpetual revenue rights. [39] [41] Post-conquest integration emphasized Maratha cavalry superiority, deploying mobile horsemen for rapid strikes that overwhelmed slower Gond defenses, while administrative reforms fused these tactics with local structures to enhance efficiency in revenue collection and fort garrisons. [39] Raghoji shifted his headquarters to Nagpur , elevating its strategic role and diminishing Devagad's prominence, as subjugated Gond kings retained nominal dues but ceded autonomy. [39] This era marked a pivot from Gond tribal governance's relative leniency toward diverse practicesâincluding lingering Islamic influences from rulers like Chand Sultanâto Bhonsle enforcement of Hindu orthodoxy, evidenced by endowments supporting traditions like Mahalaxmi worship initiated under Raghoji. [42] [43] Expansion, Conflicts, and Internal Dynamics Raghoji I Bhonsle pursued aggressive territorial expansion following his establishment of control over Nagpur in 1740, launching repeated raids into Bengal between 1741 and 1751 to enforce chauth tribute payments. These campaigns, which included the occupation of Orissa and plunder of regional wealth, yielded short-term financial gains through extorted revenues estimated in lakhs of rupees annually but provoked fierce resistance from Bengal's Nawab Alivardi Khan, resulting in prolonged guerrilla warfare and high casualties on both sides. [44] The expeditions exemplified the Bhonsles' reliance on predatory mobility, yet their logistical demandsâsustaining thousands of bargirs over vast distancesâimposed fiscal overextension, as tribute often failed to offset the costs of attrition and lost manpower. [45] Concurrent conflicts with the Peshwa and Nizam of Hyderabad further strained resources, as Nagpur forces intervened in Deccan rivalries, including support for the Nizam against Peshwa incursions in the 1750s, which diverted troops from defensive consolidation. [45] These engagements, while securing temporary alliances and border adjustments, escalated military expenditures amid fluctuating tribute systems, critiqued by contemporaries for prioritizing elite aggrandizement over sustainable governance and contributing to treasury deficits by the 1760s. [44] Proponents of Bhonsle strategy highlighted revenue innovations like intensified farming contracts to fund armies, yet empirical outcomes revealed vulnerabilities, as overreliance on distant plundering eroded local agrarian stability amid heavy exactions. [46] Internal dynamics destabilized the state post-Raghoji I's death in 1755, with succession contested among sons Janoji, Mudhoji, and Sabaji, prompting Peshwa arbitration that installed Janoji as ruler while allocating auxiliary roles to siblings, fostering latent resentments. [45] Janoji's reign until 1772 saw palace factions, including ministers like Devajipant aligned against Mudhoji's claims of seniority via maternal lineage, eroding administrative cohesion through intrigue and proxy skirmishes. [47] Janoji's death triggered open civil war, resolved by Mudhoji's decisive victory at the Battle of Panchgaon in 1772, where he killed Sabaji, consolidating power but at the expense of territorial partitions imposed by Peshwa mediators, which fragmented authority and invited external meddling. [44] These fratricidal struggles, while enabling Mudhoji's revenue stabilization efforts through reassessments, perpetuated cycles of vengeance and weakened military readiness against peripheral threats. [45] Achievements in Infrastructure and Economy The Bhonsle rulers invested in fortifications to safeguard Nagpur as a strategic hub, with Raghoji I Bhonsle strengthening the pre-existing Nagpur Fort after his 1743 conquest, transforming it into a fortified palace complex that anchored administrative control and protected vital trade corridors linking central India to coastal ports. These enhancements, including bastioned walls and outposts, facilitated secure merchant transit amid regional instability, elevating Nagpur 's role as an inland emporium by the mid-18th century. [48] Economically, the Bhonsles encouraged agricultural expansion in the Deccan black soils, where cotton emerged as a key cash crop alongside staples like millet and pulses, supporting revenue through land assessments that incentivized cultivation across an estimated 10-15 million acres under their domain by the late 1700s. [49] Market towns proliferated along trade arteries, drawing Gujarati and Marwari merchants to handle cotton ginning and export, which bolstered a nascent commercial class and positioned Nagpur as a nexus for overland commerce in textiles and grains prior to intensified British involvement. [34] Yet these gains masked structural frailties, as fiscal reliance on plunderâexemplified by Raghoji I's repeated Bengal incursions yielding annual chauth tributes equivalent to millions in contemporary rupeesâprioritized extractive raids over enduring productive systems, resulting in episodic booms untethered to institutional reforms like standardized banking or irrigation networks. [50] Debt burdens escalated under successors, with tribute shortfalls and tribute obligations compounding into unsustainable liabilities by the early 19th century , underscoring a predatory model vulnerable to military reversals rather than self-sustaining growth. [51] British Colonial Period Subsidiary Alliance and Anglo-Maratha Wars The subsidiary alliance system, formalized for the Nagpur state through the Treaty of Deogaon on December 17, 1803, compelled Raghoji II Bhonsle to cede Cuttack, Balasore, and territories west of the Wardha River while agreeing to host a British subsidiary force funded by his revenues. [52] [53] This arrangement, imposed after Bhonsle defeats in the Second Anglo-Maratha Warâincluding the Battle of Argaon on November 29, 1803ârestricted Nagpur's foreign relations and military autonomy, ostensibly providing protection against external threats but effectively establishing British oversight over internal decisions. [53] [54] British proponents, such as Governor-General Lord Wellesley, framed the alliance as a stabilizing measure amid Maratha confederacy rivalries and potential French influences, yet it functioned as a mechanism for fiscal extraction and strategic encirclement, eroding the ruler's sovereignty by requiring approval for alliances and prohibiting independent armies beyond fixed limits. [54] Under Raghoji II's rule until his death on March 22, 1816, the alliance strained Nagpur's resources, as the subsidy paymentsâequivalent to maintaining 5,000â6,000 British troopsâdiverted funds from local administration and military upkeep, fostering dependency and internal discontent. [54] His successor, Appa Sahib Bhonsle (r. 1816â1818), initially reaffirmed the treaty but chafed under Resident Richard Jenkins ' influence, viewing the system as predatory interference that undermined Maratha prestige and autonomy. [55] Maratha chroniclers and later analyses portray the alliance not as mutual benefit but as coerced subordination, with British garrisons in key forts like Sitabuldi enabling surveillance and preemptive interventions, contrasting sharply with official British narratives of benevolent guardianship. [54] Tensions escalated into the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817â1818) when Appa Sahib aligned with Peshwa Baji Rao II's uprising against British paramountcy, attacking the Nagpur residency on October 29, 1817, and mobilizing forces against subsidiary troops. [55] British retaliation culminated in the Battle of Sitabuldi on November 27, 1817, where 1,300 British and allied sepoys under Colonel John Scott repelled 20,000â30,000 Bhonsle troops, securing the fort after intense artillery exchanges and infantry assaults. [55] [53] Subsequent campaigns, including General John Doveton's victory at the Juuljulee hills in January 1818, dismantled Bhonsle resistance, leading to territorial cessions of Saugor, Nerbudda valleys, and parts of Gondwana , further entrenching subsidiary control. [53] Appa Sahib's defeat exposed the alliance's fragility as a tool of dominance rather than defense, with British forces leveraging superior discipline and logisticsâtotaling over 100,000 troops across the warâto suppress Maratha coalitions, while Maratha accounts decry the conflict as an inevitable backlash to incremental sovereignty loss. [55] [54] Annexation of 1853 and Doctrinal Lapse Raghuji III Bhonsle, the Maharaja of Nagpur, died on December 11, 1853, without a natural or formally adopted heir, prompting the British East India Company, under Governor-General Lord Dalhousie, to apply the Doctrine of Lapse for annexation. [56] The doctrine, formalized in the late 1840s, stipulated that princely states lacking a direct male heir would eschew recognition of adoptions unless pre-approved by British authorities, reverting control to the Company rather than permitting succession. [57] This policy, absent explicit sanction in prior treaties with Nagpur dating to the 1818 subsidiary alliance , enabled Dalhousie to claim the state's revenues, territories, and assets, expanding British dominion over approximately 80,000 square miles and a population exceeding 3 million. [57] [56] Following the annexation proclamation on December 21, 1853, British forces under Commissioner Robert Hamilton seized the Nagpur durbar, confiscating royal treasures valued at millions of rupees, including the famed Bhonsle jewels and an estimated 30 million rupees in state funds, which were transported to Calcutta. [58] These actions, justified by Company officials as recovering debts from prior Bhonsle loans and lapsed revenues, ignited immediate local resentments among nobility , zamindars, and military retainers, who viewed the seizures as predatory rather than administrative. [58] Sporadic protests erupted in Nagpur city and surrounding talukas, with former court officials petitioning for restitution, though suppressed by British troops without widespread violence in 1853â54. [57] The annexation's coercive execution fueled latent anti-colonial grievances, manifesting in Nagpur's alignment with the 1857 Indian Rebellion, where local sepoys from the Nagpur contingent mutinied in June 1857, joining broader uprisings by dispossessed elites and echoing the Doctrine's role in eroding princely legitimacy across annexed states like Jhansi and Satara. [59] Causal links trace to the policy's disruption of traditional hierarchies, as evidenced by participant testimonies citing heir disinheritances as provocations for unified resistance against Company overreach. [59] British reprisals in Nagpur quelled the unrest by July 1857, but the events underscored how lapse annexations primed regional instability. [59] Critiquing the Doctrine of Lapse reveals it as a doctrinal contrivance masking expansionist opportunism , diverging from era-specific international norms that tolerated conquest but not systematic subversion of indigenous succession customs; Hindu law , as interpreted in pre-colonial precedents, permitted adoptions to perpetuate lineages, a flexibility British selectively ignored to fabricate "lapsed" claims absent mutual treaty obligations. [57] While balanced against Bhonsle precedents of fiscal mismanagementâevident in Raghuji III's era through chronic debts exceeding 2 crore rupees and administrative inefficienciesâthe annexation prioritized territorial gain over reform, forgoing options like regency or conditional adoption as applied elsewhere. [57] Contemporary British critics, including civil servants in Dalhousie's councils, decried the policy's ethical overreach, arguing it breached good-faith subsidiary pacts and provoked foreseeable backlash, though pro-annexation advocates cited state solvency needs without empirical proof of imminent collapse. [57] This lapse, in essence, exemplified causal realism in imperial strategy: a legal veneer rationalizing power asymmetries rather than principled governance . [57] Administration as Capital of Central Provinces In 1861, the British administration established the Central Provinces by combining the Saugor and Nerbudda Territories with the Nagpur Province, designating Nagpur as the capital to leverage its central location for efficient governance over the expansive region. [60] This shift centralized administrative functions in Nagpur , leading to the development of civil lines âsegregated residential areas for British officialsâand key public buildings to support the provincial secretariat and judiciary. [61] The Bengal Nagpur Railway's extension reached Nagpur between 1880 and 1882, linking it to networks like Rajnandgaon and facilitating trade and troop movements, though the system's guaranteed returnsâoften double those in Britainâensured profits flowed primarily to British investors via repatriation , underscoring its extractive orientation rather than purely developmental intent. [62] [63] In tandem, responses to recurrent famines, including severe ones in the Central Provinces during 1896â1897 and 1899â1900, involved codifying famine relief procedures and advancing irrigation infrastructure, such as canals, to avert total crop failures and enable emergency public works for affected populations. [64] [61] Land revenue assessments, often rigid under malguzari and ryotwari variants prevalent in the province, imposed escalating demands that exacerbated peasant indebtedness and distress, particularly amid fluctuating agricultural yields, as documented in analyses of colonial fiscal pressures in Central India . [65] Culturally, British initiatives promoted English-medium education and Christian missionary schools in Nagpur , aiming to cultivate a class of intermediaries, yet these encountered pushback through Hindu revivalist efforts, including Arya Samaj branches that emphasized Vedic learning and social reform to counter proselytization. [61] [66] Berar's administrative integration in 1903 further solidified Nagpur 's role, extending oversight to additional territories while perpetuating revenue extraction to fund imperial priorities. [60] 20th Century and Independence Role in Indian Independence Movement The Nagpur session of the Indian National Congress , held from December 27 to 30, 1920, marked a pivotal endorsement of Mahatma Gandhi's Non-Cooperation Movement, with C. Vijayaraghavachariar presiding and a resolution moved by C.R. Das urging boycotts of British institutions, titles, and schools to protest post-World War I policies like the Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh massacre . [67] [68] This gathering, attended by over 14,000 delegates, shifted Congress toward mass mobilization , reducing membership fees to one rupee to broaden participation among lower classes and formalizing Gandhi's leadership amid debates with moderates like Motilal Nehru . [69] [70] In parallel, Nagpur emerged as a center for alternative nationalist ideologies emphasizing Hindu cultural revival, exemplified by the founding of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh ( RSS ) on September 27, 1925, by physician Keshav Baliram Hedgewar during Vijayadashami at his residence in the city's Sukravari neighborhood. [71] Hedgewar, influenced by prior communal riots including a 1923 Hindu-Muslim clash in Nagpur that underscored divisions, established the RSS to foster disciplined Hindu youth through daily shakhas focused on physical training, character building, and national unity, critiquing Congress's approach for insufficiently addressing Hindu disorganization amid threats from proselytizing and potential partition-like fragmentations. [72] [73] The organization's non-electoral, volunteer-based model prioritized long-term societal resilience over immediate political agitation, drawing initial recruits from local akhadas and contrasting with socialist-leaning factions by rejecting class warfare in favor of integrated cultural nationalism . [71] During the Quit India Movement launched on August 8, 1942, Nagpur witnessed widespread protests, strikes, and sabotage against British rule, with local Congress leaders and RSS affiliates forming underground networks to distribute propaganda, disrupt railways, and organize hartals despite mass arrests exceeding 100,000 nationwide. [74] Key figures, including RSS swayamsevaks like those imprisoned in Nagpur Central Jail for satyagraha and anti-colonial actions, contributed to administrative paralysis, as evidenced by over 50,000 combined arrests from prior movements amplified in 1942's scale. [75] [76] These efforts, blending Gandhian civil disobedience with covert operations, eroded British control in the Central Provinces by sustaining resistance post the internment of top Congress leadership on August 9. [77] Post-Partition Reorganization and Vidarbha Integration Following independence in 1947, the Central Provinces and Berar province, which included the Vidarbha region with Nagpur as a key center, underwent administrative reorganization. On October 25, 1950, it was formally reconstituted as the State of Madhya Pradesh under the Constitution of India , retaining Nagpur as the state capital due to its established administrative infrastructure and central location. This integration placed the predominantly Marathi-speaking Vidarbha districtsâhistorically distinct through their Berar and Central Provinces legacyâunder a larger entity dominated by Hindi-speaking areas, fostering early debates on regional autonomy . [78] The States Reorganisation Commission (SRC), appointed in 1953 and reporting in 1955 under Justice Fazl Ali , examined demands for redrawing state boundaries primarily on linguistic lines while considering administrative viability. Vidarbha leaders submitted memoranda advocating a separate state, citing deep-rooted regional consciousness, distinct cultural identity, and potential economic self-sufficiency through resources like cotton production and emerging industries in Nagpur . The SRC recognized this consciousness, noting it as conceded even by integration proponents, but ultimately recommended against immediate separation to prioritize larger, linguistically cohesive units for efficient governance and resource pooling; however, the government's implementation via the States Reorganisation Act of 1956 rejected standalone Vidarbha statehood, maintaining the region's inclusion in the enlarged, bilingual Madhya Pradesh . This decision stemmed from concerns over fragmenting states excessively and diluting administrative capacity, though it intensified local sentiments of marginalization. [79] Post-1956, economic disparities within Madhya Pradesh highlighted Vidarbha's challenges, with the region contributing significantly to cotton outputâaccounting for a substantial share of the state's agricultural exportsâbut experiencing slower industrial expansion compared to central Hindi heartlands like Bhopal . By the late 1950s, Nagpur hosted textile mills and small-scale manufacturing, yet overall investment lagged, attributed by regional analysts to centralized planning favoring northern districts and inadequate infrastructure like irrigation , leading to critiques of state-level neglect that exacerbated rural distress and urban underdevelopment . Proponents of integration argued that affiliation with a larger Madhya Pradesh enabled access to broader fiscal resources and unified planning under Five-Year Plans, potentially mitigating isolation; regionalists countered that this diluted Vidarbha's distinct priorities, risking cultural erosion through Hindi imposition in administration and education , and perpetuating economic lag by diverting funds away from local needs. These tensions fueled ongoing statehood advocacy, emphasizing Vidarbha's historical self-governance under British rule as a basis for tailored development over subsumption in a mismatched larger unit. [80] Post-Independence Developments Formation of Maharashtra and State Capital Status The Bombay Reorganisation Act of 1960, enacted by the Parliament of India , bifurcated the bilingual Bombay State into the Marathi-majority state of Maharashtra and the Gujarati-majority state of Gujarat , effective May 1, 1960, thereby integrating the Vidarbha regionâformerly part of the Central Provinces and Berar âinto the newly formed Maharashtra . [81] [82] This merger incorporated Nagpur , which had briefly lost its capital status after states' reorganization in 1956 , as the designated winter capital under terms of the Nagpur Pact signed on September 28, 1953, which aimed to protect Vidarbha 's interests by stipulating annual legislative sessions in the city and equitable resource allocation. [83] [84] Immediate governance shifts positioned Mumbai as the primary administrative hub for budget and monsoon sessions of the Maharashtra Legislative Assembly , while Nagpur hosted the winter session, typically lasting at least six weeks as per the pact's provisions, with the Governor maintaining a secondary residence there to facilitate proceedings. [85] [86] This dual-capital arrangement sought to decentralize decision-making and address Vidarbha's historical autonomy, though implementation relied on executive adherence rather than statutory enforcement. [83] In parallel, early post-formation infrastructure initiatives included the establishment of the Visvesvaraya Regional College of Engineering (later VNIT) in June 1960, sponsored jointly by the Governments of India and Maharashtra through amalgamation of existing technical institutions in Nagpur , signaling investment in regional technical education amid broader state-building efforts. [87] However, these measures occurred against persistent challenges like water scarcity in Nagpur , which predated and continued beyond the merger without immediate resolution. [88] Critics, drawing from observed developmental patterns, have argued that administrative power centralized in Mumbai fostered regional inequalities, with Vidarbha receiving disproportionate underinvestment relative to promises of balanced growth, as evidenced by subsequent economic data showing lower per capita income and infrastructure deficits compared to western Maharashtra . [88] [89] Economic and Urban Growth in Late 20th Century During the late 20th century , Nagpur's economy experienced moderate expansion driven primarily by agricultural specialization in oranges and limited industrial initiatives, though these were hampered by overreliance on public sector employment and vulnerability to market fluctuations. Orange cultivation, which positioned Nagpur as a key horticultural hub, saw steady growth from the 1970s onward, with the district's production contributing significantly to Maharashtra's output; by the 1990s, Vidarbha region's orange orchards covered expanding acreage, supported by favorable climate and initial government extension services, yet this monoculture approach fostered risks from pests, erratic rainfall, and price crashes without diversified cropping. [90] Industrial development remained subdued, with public sector undertakings like the Ordnance Factory and textile units providing stable but low-growth employment, while the establishment of the Butibori industrial area in 1984 aimed to attract manufacturing, though private investment lagged due to infrastructural deficits and policy bottlenecks favoring state-led initiatives over market-driven expansion. Urban growth accelerated amid these economic patterns, with Nagpur's municipal population rising from approximately 1.3 million in 1981 to over 1.6 million by 1991, reflecting a decadal increase of about 25%, fueled by in-migration from rural Vidarbha districts plagued by agrarian distress. This tripling of urban population between the 1970s and 2000âreaching around 2 million by the early 2000sâstrained housing and services, as migrants sought non-farm jobs in government administration and small-scale trade, underscoring causal links between rural vulnerabilities and cityward flows rather than robust pull factors like industrial booms. [91] The orange sector's booms in the 1980s and 1990s , marked by rising yields and domestic market penetration, masked underlying fragilities; farmers faced indebtedness from high input costs and unseasonal losses, exacerbating suicides in Vidarbha , where reports from the 1990s documented hundreds of cases annually tied to crop failures and loan defaults, highlighting how monoculture dependency undermined long-term resilience without complementary irrigation or credit reforms. Public sector dominance, while anchoring urban stability through salaried positions in railways and defense, perpetuated inefficiencies, as bureaucratic hiring absorbed labor without fostering innovation, contributing to sluggish per capita income growth compared to Maharashtra's coastal hubs. [92] [93] Contemporary Challenges and Transformations Nagpur, as the headquarters of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh ( RSS ) since its founding in 1925, has served as a focal point for Hindu nationalist activities, including annual Vijayadashami events that draw thousands and amplify discussions on Hindutva ideology. [94] [95] In October 2025, the RSS marked its centenary at the Nagpur headquarters with speeches by chief Mohan Bhagwat addressing national security and cultural identity, underscoring the organization's influence on local discourse amid broader political alignments with the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). [96] This role has intersected with communal tensions rooted in historical grievances, particularly resentment toward Mughal-era figures like Aurangzeb , documented for policies involving temple destructions and forced conversions in the Deccan region. [97] These tensions erupted into violence on March 17, 2025, when protests by groups including the Vishwa Hindu Parishad (VHP) and Bajrang Dal demanding the removal of Aurangzeb's tomb in Nagpur led to clashes, vehicle arson, and a citywide curfew . [98] [99] The unrest, which injured dozens and prompted prohibitory orders in areas like Mahal and Gandhibagh, reflected demands to replace the site with a memorial to local Maratha rulers, highlighting persistent local memory of Islamist conquests' destructive legacy rather than sanitized narratives. [100] [101] Authorities imposed restrictions after stones were pelted and effigies burned, with the VHP denying instigation but advocating historical rectification, while critics attributed the flare-up to orchestrated polarization amid rising scrutiny of Mughal symbols nationwide. [102] [103] Infrastructure development has advanced with the Nagpur Metro Rail project, operational since 2019 on Phase 1 lines totaling 40.3 km, aimed at alleviating traffic in a city of over 2.5 million residents. [104] However, the project has incurred mounting losses, escalating from INR 2.90 crore in 2016-17 to INR 178.58 crore by 2020-21, fueled by overestimated ridership and operational shortfalls, alongside criticisms of high debt burdens on state finances exceeding INR 6,700 crore for expansions. [104] [105] Phase 2 works, approved in 2020 with broad-gauge integration, face delays from bureaucratic hurdles and funding gaps, contributing to uneven benefits where peripheral areas lag despite central government equity of 50%. [106] [107] Persistent regional neglect has fueled the Vidarbha statehood movement, with advocates citing a developmental backlog of Rs 75,000 crore in irrigation and infrastructure , as Vidarbha âcomprising 31.6% of Maharashtra's areaâreceives disproportionately low investments relative to its resource contributions like cotton and power generation. [108] Farmer suicides underscore agrarian distress, with 1,051 cases in the Amravati division alone in 2024 out of Maharashtra's 2,635 total, linked to incomplete irrigation projects covering under 20% of cultivable land despite promises. [109] Groups like the Vidarbha Rajya Andolan Samiti (VRAS) have intensified protests, including a 2024 Nagpur march detaining 350 participants, arguing that separation would enable targeted governance to reverse rural exodus and stunted growth, though opponents highlight fiscal viability concerns. [110] [111] Broader urban strains, including stalled projects amid 2025 floods from unauthorized constructions and inadequate sewerage, compound these transformations, balancing ambitious plans like a 1,780-acre commercial district against basics like water supply deficits. Click Here TheNewsDirt All Posts Politics Opinion Sport Entertainment Vidarbha News Everyday Struggles City Stories History Vidarbha Vidarbha Spotlight Daily Dirt Guest Post Search The History of Nagpur: From Prehistoric Times to the Bhosale Dynasty Pranay Arya Oct 24, 2024 8 min read Updated: Feb 12 Rated NaN out of 5 stars. Nagpur, the city we know today, is rich with history and culture that goes back thousands of years. It has witnessed different phases of human development, from the early days of prehistoric times, through ancient mythology, to the rule of powerful dynasties like the Bhosale family. Each phase of history has shaped Nagpur into the city it is now. We will take a journey through these important phases, starting from the prehistoric period and moving through the Bhosale dynasty’s rule. Prehistoric Nagpur: A Land of Early Settlements Prehistoric Nagpur Stone Age and Early Tools Nagpur's history goes back to the Stone Age, a period when human beings used stone tools for survival. This period, known as the prehistoric period, can be divided into three phases: the Stone Age, the Copper Age, and the Iron Age. In the Stone Age, human beings lived by hunting animals and gathering food from plants. The region around Nagpur, particularly areas like Kalameshwar and Navegaon, has yielded a significant number of tools from this period. These tools were mainly made of stone and were used for hunting, cutting, and other daily survival activities. Archaeologists have discovered these tools in various parts of Nagpur, showing that the region was inhabited by early human beings. The tools found from this time are simple in design but were very important for the people who used them. These early settlers were nomadic, moving from one place to another in search of food and shelter. They lived in caves and temporary shelters made of natural materials like branches and leaves. The Copper Age and Advancements in Technology After the Stone Age, human beings began to develop better tools. This marked the beginning of the Copper Age. During this period, stone tools were slowly replaced with tools made of copper. Copper was a much stronger material and could be shaped into more effective tools for hunting and farming. This period is also significant because it marks the beginning of settled life. People started to form small communities and began farming. They no longer had to rely entirely on hunting and gathering for food. In the Nagpur region, many copper weapons and tools have been found. These include knives, spearheads, and other implements that were used for both hunting and farming. More than 400 copper weapons have been found near Nagpur, indicating that this region was rich in copper and that people were skilled in metalworking. The Iron Age and Permanent Settlements The next major phase in human development was the Iron Age. In this period, people started using iron to make tools. Iron is even stronger than copper, which allowed people to make better tools for farming and warfare. By this time, people had started to live in permanent settlements, farming the land and raising animals. The Iron Age saw the rise of more complex societies, with rules and leadership structures. In Nagpur, archaeological digs have revealed many iron tools. These tools were used in farming, building, and everyday life. Settlements from this time have been found near Koradi, Kohli, Gondighogar, and other nearby areas. These early communities built stone houses, some of which still stand as protected monuments today. Mythology of Nagpur: Legends and Ancient Tales Nagpur is not only important for its prehistoric history but also for its connection to ancient Indian mythology. Many ancient texts and legends mention the region of Vidarbha, which includes Nagpur. These stories are an important part of Nagpur’s cultural and historical identity. The Origins of Vidarbha The region of Vidarbha, where Nagpur is located, is mentioned in many ancient Indian texts, including the Aitareya Brahmana and the Mahabharata. Vidarbha was known as a kingdom of skilled hunters and warriors. According to legend, the region got its name from a person named Vidarbha, a member of the ancient Yadava dynasty. The Yadavas were an ancient tribe that ruled parts of central India, and Vidarbha is said to be one of their most important regions. Krishna and Rukmini In the epic Mahabharata, Vidarbha is ruled by King Bhishmaka, who is the father of Rukmini. Rukmini was the princess who married Lord Krishna, one of the most revered figures in Hindu mythology. The story of Rukmini and Krishna’s marriage is a significant part of Vidarbha’s cultural heritage. According to the legend, Rukmini fell in love with Krishna and sent him a letter asking him to rescue her from an unwanted marriage. Krishna came to Vidarbha, fought off her suitors, and took her away to marry her. The Naga Connection to Nagpur Another important part of Nagpur’s mythology is its connection to the Nagas, a serpent-worshiping tribe. The Nagas were a powerful tribe in ancient India, and many places in central India, including Nagpur, are believed to be named after them. The Nagas were known for their bravery and their devotion to their serpent deities. Nagpur, in particular, is believed to have been an important center for Naga worship. The city’s name itself is thought to come from the word "Naga," reflecting this ancient connection. Many local legends speak of the Nagas ruling this area before other dynasties took over. The Ramayana and Nagpur Another significant mythological connection is to the Ramayana, one of the most important epics in Indian literature. It is believed that Lord Rama visited the Vidarbha region during his exile from Ayodhya. According to legend, it was during this time that Lord Rama stayed near Nagpur and visited the Ramtek region. The Ram Mandir at Ramtek is believed to have been built to honor Lord Rama’s visit to this region. This connection to the Ramayana adds to the cultural significance of Nagpur. The Ramtek temple is one of the oldest and most important religious sites in the region and continues to be a place of pilgrimage for many devotees. The Bhosale Dynasty: The Rise of a Maratha Powerhouse in Nagpur Rise of the Bhosle After centuries of mythological and prehistoric development, Nagpur’s history took a significant turn with the arrival of the Bhosale dynasty in the 18th century. The Bhosales were part of the larger Maratha Empire, which was one of the most powerful empires in India at the time. The Bhosale family’s rule in Nagpur marks one of the most important periods in the city’s history. The Early Days of the Bhosale Dynasty The Bhosale dynasty’s connection to Nagpur began with Parsoji Bhosale, the founder of the Nagpur branch of the Maratha Empire. Parsoji was a trusted officer under the Maratha ruler Chhatrapati Shivaji, and he played an important role in collecting taxes (known as "chauth") from the region of Vidarbha. This marked the beginning of the Bhosale family’s influence in the region. After Parsoji’s death in 1709, his son Kanhoji Bhosale succeeded him as the ruler of Nagpur. However, the real rise of the Bhosale dynasty came under Kanhoji’s nephew, Raghuji I. Raghuji was a powerful and ambitious ruler, and it was under his leadership that Nagpur became a significant center of Maratha power. Raghuji Bhosale I: Expansion and Consolidation Raghuji Bhosale I is considered one of the most important rulers of the Bhosale dynasty. He was known for his military campaigns and his efforts to expand the Maratha Empire into central and eastern India. Raghuji’s rule marked a period of great growth and prosperity for Nagpur. One of Raghuji’s most significant achievements was his conquest of Bengal. Raghuji led a series of successful military campaigns in Bengal, Orissa, and parts of northern India. His campaigns were so successful that he was able to collect taxes from these regions, further strengthening his power. Under Raghuji’s rule, Nagpur became a well-administered kingdom with strong defenses and a thriving economy. Raghuji also focused on public works and infrastructure, building roads, temples, and other public buildings that contributed to the growth of Nagpur as an important city. Raghuji’s Contribution to Culture and Religion Raghuji was not only a great military leader but also a patron of religion and culture. One of his most famous contributions was the restoration of the Ram Mandir at Ramtek. This temple, dedicated to Lord Rama, is one of the oldest and most important temples in the region. Raghuji’s restoration of the temple further strengthened Nagpur’s connection to its mythological roots and reinforced his image as a pious and righteous ruler. Internal Struggles and Conflicts Despite his successes, Raghuji’s rule was not without challenges. After his death, his four sons—Janoji, Mudhoji, Sabaji, and Nibaji—began to fight over the control of the kingdom. This led to internal strife, weakening the Bhosale dynasty’s hold on power. The family feuds continued for several years, making it difficult for the dynasty to present a united front against external threats. The British Threat and the Second Maratha War Second Maratha War While the Bhosales were dealing with internal issues, a new and powerful threat was emerging from the east—the British East India Company. By the late 18th century, the British were rapidly expanding their control over India, and central India was one of their key targets. The Bhosales found themselves in direct conflict with the British during the Second Maratha War, which began in 1803. Janoji Bhosale, with the help of other Maratha leaders like Daulatrao Shinde, tried to resist the British forces, but the Maratha Empire was already in decline. The British, under the leadership of Lord Wellesley, launched a series of successful campaigns that severely weakened the Marathas. The Treaty of Devgaon and the Decline of the Bhosale Dynasty Treaty of Devgaon After suffering defeats in battle, the Bhosales were forced to sign the Treaty of Devgaon in 1803. This treaty marked a turning point in the history of the Bhosale dynasty. Under the terms of the treaty, the Bhosales had to cede several important territories to the British, including the region of Orissa. This significantly reduced the Bhosale dynasty’s power and marked the beginning of their decline. The treaty also imposed strict limitations on the Bhosales’ military capabilities, further weakening their ability to defend their kingdom. Over time, the British tightened their control over the Bhosale dynasty, turning them into little more than puppet rulers. The Tragic Death of Parsoji Bhosale and Appasaheb’s Rise After Raghuji II’s death, his son Parsoji Bhosale ascended the throne. However, Parsoji was not a strong ruler. He was weak in both body and mind, which made him an easy target for ambitious rivals. One such rival was his cousin, Appasaheb (also known as Mudhoji). Appasaheb quickly began to position himself as the real power behind the throne. He conspired with several Maratha chieftains and took control of Nagpur by placing Parsoji under his guardianship. Parsoji’s reign was short-lived, and he was soon found dead under mysterious circumstances. It is widely believed that he was strangled to death, although the true cause of his death remains unknown. Appasaheb’s Defiance and the Battle of Sitabuldi Battle of Sitaburdi With Parsoji out of the way, Appasaheb Bhosale became the ruler of Nagpur. He immediately set about consolidating power and strengthening his kingdom. However, Appasaheb’s ambitions soon brought him into direct conflict with the British. In 1817, Appasaheb launched a military campaign against the British, attacking the Residency in Nagpur. This led to the famous Battle of Sitabuldi, one of the most significant battles in the history of Nagpur. Appasaheb’s forces fought bravely, but they were ultimately defeated by the British. The defeat marked the end of Appasaheb’s rule and the beginning of full British control over Nagpur. The End of the Bhosale Dynasty and the British Annexation of Nagpur British Annex Nagpur After his defeat, Appasaheb was captured and imprisoned by the British. With Appasaheb out of the way, the British took full control of Nagpur. In 1854, after the death of Raghuji III, who died without an heir, the British officially annexed Nagpur under the Doctrine of Lapse. This marked the end of the Bhosale dynasty’s rule over Nagpur. Legacy of Nagpur and the Bhosale Dynasty Nagpur’s history, from its prehistoric roots to its role in the Maratha Empire, reflects the city’s importance in India’s cultural and political landscape. Today, Nagpur continues to thrive as a major city, but its past remains a vital part of its identity. The history of Nagpur is one of evolution, from its early days as a prehistoric settlement to its rise as a powerful kingdom under the Bhosale dynasty. It has witnessed the changes of time, from ancient mythology to colonial rule. The Bhosale dynasty’s contributions, along with the city's deep mythological roots, have shaped Nagpur into what it is today. Through prehistoric discoveries, ancient legends, and the legacy of the Bhosale dynasty, Nagpur has maintained its place in history as a region rich in culture, power, and resilience.         Maharashtra. Maharashtra » Maharashtra Cities » Nagpur » History of Nagpur History of Nagpur Gond prince of Deogad kingdom, Bhakt Buland, founded
        Nagpur in the early 18th century in the Chhindwara district. He tried to
        change the life of Nagpur as his new capital after seeing the advantage
        of civilized life of Delhi. His successor Chand Sultan too continued the
        work of Bhakt Buland. Disputes regarding succession arose with the death
        of Chand Sultan in 1739. Maratha governor of Berar, Raghuji Bhonsle, tried to restore his elder
        son to the throne, and the control of Nagpur slowly passed on from the
        Gonds to the Marathas. Later Nagpur became the capital of the Bhonsles.
        Bhonsles lost to the British and Nagpur came under British influence in
        1817. Raghuji III died without leaving any heir in 1853. As a result,
        the city came under the full control of British under Lord Dalhousie's
        Doctrine of Lapse. Nagpur became the capital of the Central Provinces of India in 1861.
        With the advent of the Great Indian Peninsula Railway (GIP) in 1867, its
        development spurred as a trade centre. After Indian independence, Nagpur became the capital of Madhya Bharat
        state (C.P. and Berar). In 1960, the Marathi majority Vidarbha region
        was merged with the new state of Maharashtra and Nagpur was designated
        the second capital of Maharashtra state, alternating with Bombay as the
        seat of the Maharashtra state legislature. Find sources: "History of Nagpur" – news · newspapers · books · scholar · JSTOR ( May 2012 ) ( Learn how and when to remove this message ) Aspect of Indian history The history of Nagpur , in central India , spans over 5,000 years, including the Kingdom of Nagpur in the 18th and 19th century. Human existence around present-day Nagpur city (in Maharashtra , India) can be traced back 3,000 years to the 8th century BC. Menhir burial sites at Drugdhamna (near Mhada colony) indicate megalithic culture existed around Nagpur and is still followed in present times. [ 1 ] The first reference to the name "Nagpur" is found in a 10th-century copper-plate inscription discovered at Devali in the neighbouring Wardha district. The inscription is a record of grant of a village situated in the visaya (district) of Nagpura-Nandivardhana during time of Rastrakuta king Krsna III in the Saka year 862 (940 CE). [ 2 ] [ 3 ] Inscription found at Ramtek show that during the 12th century AD Nagpur and its surrounding regions formed the part of the thickly wooded country called Jhadimandala under Yadavas of Devagiri. [ 4 ] However, tradition ascribes the founding of Nagpur to Bakht Buland Shah , a prince of the Gond kingdom of Deogarh in the Chhindwara district . In 1743, the Maratha leader Raghoji Bhonsale of Vidarbha established himself at Nagpur, after conquering the territories of Deogarh, Chanda and Chhattisgarh by 1751. After Raghoji's death in 1755, his son and successor Janoji was forced to acknowledge the effective supremacy of the Maratha Peshwa of Pune in 1769. Regardless, the Nagpur state continued to grow. Janoji's successor Mudhoji I Bhonsale (d. 1788) came to power in 1785 and bought Mandla and the upper Narmada valley from the Peshwa between 1796 and 1798, after which Raghoji II Bhonsale (d. 1816) acquired Hoshangabad , the larger part of Saugor and Damoh . Under Raghoji II, Nagpur covered what is now the east of Maharashtra, Chhattisgarh, Orissa , and parts of Madhya Pradesh and Jharkhand . In 1803 Raghoji II joined the Peshwas against the British in the Second Anglo-Maratha War . The British prevailed, and Raghoji was forced to cede Cuttack , Sambalpur , and part of Berar . After Raghoji II's death in 1816, his son Parsaji was deposed and murdered by Mudhoji II Bhonsale . Despite the fact that he had entered into a treaty with the British in the same year, Mudhoji joined the Peshwa in the Third Anglo-Maratha War in 1817 against the British, but was forced to cede the rest of Berar to the Nizam of Hyderabad , and parts of Saugor and Damoh, Mandla , Betul , Seoni and the Narmada valley to the British after suffering a defeat at Sitabuldi in modern-day Nagpur city. The Sitabuldi fort was the site of a fierce battle between the British and the Bhonsale of Nagpur in 1817. The battle was a turning point as it laid the foundations of the downfall of the Bhonsales and paved the way for the British acquisition of Nagpur city. [ 5 ] Mudhoji was deposed after a temporary restoration to the throne, after which the British placed Raghoji III Bhonsale the grandchild of Raghoji II, on the throne. During the rule of Raghoji III (which lasted till 1853), the region was administered by a British resident. In 1854 the British annexed Nagpur, after Raghoji III had died some months before without leaving an heir. Central Provinces and Berar, 1903. Princely states are shown in yellow. In 1861, the Nagpur Province (which consisted of the present Nagpur region, Chhindwara, and Chhattisgarh and existed from 1854 to 1861) became part of the Central Provinces and came under the administration of a commissioner under the British central government, with Nagpur as its capital. Tata Group started the country's first textile mill at Nagpur, [ 6 ] formally known as Central India Spinning and Weaving Company Ltd. The company was popularly known as "Empress Mills" as it was inaugurated on 1 January 1877, the day Queen Victoria was proclaimed Empress of India. Hislop college was the first and foremost college in Nagpur and it was established in 1846. In June 1885, the second college in Nagpur was established, the Morris College, Nagpur , and it was the first government college. All Saints Cathedral is the first Anglican Church. Bishop Cotton School is the first school which was established by Anglicans in Nagpur. References are to be found in The History of All Saints Cathedral. Berar was added in 1903. Political activity in Nagpur during India's freedom struggle included hosting of two annual sessions of the Indian National Congress . The Non-cooperation movement was launched in the Nagpur session of 1920. In August 1923, the University of Nagpur was established by the education department of Central Province Government. In 1925, K. B. Hedgewar founded RSS , a Hindu nationalist organization in Nagpur with an idea of creating a Hindu nation . After Indian Independence in 1947, Central Provinces and Berar became a province of India, and in 1950 became the Indian state of Madhya Pradesh , again with Nagpur as its capital. However, when the Indian states were reorganized along linguistic lines in 1956, the Nagpur region and Berar were transferred to Bombay state , which in 1960 was split between the states of Maharashtra and Gujarat . At a formal public ceremony on 14 October 1956 in Nagpur, B. R. Ambedkar along with his supporters converted to Buddhism starting Dalit Buddhist movement which is still active. In 1994, the city witnessed its most violent day in modern times due to the Gowari stampede deaths . References [ edit ] ↑ "3000-year-old burial site unearthed" . The Times of India . 2 March 2008 .
